etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French event, from Latin ēventus (“an event, occurrence”), from ēveniō (“to happen, to fall out, to come out”), from ē (“out of, from”), short form of ex + veniō (“come”); related to venture, advent, convent, invent, convene, evene, etc.

quote.citation: 1856 February, [Thomas Babington] Macaulay, “Oliver Goldsmith”, in T[homas] F[lower] E[llis], editor, The Miscellaneous Writings and Speeches of Lord Macaulay, new edition, London: Longman, Green, Reader, & Dyer, published 1871, →OCLC:
quote.text: the events of his early years

quote.citation: 2017, Anthony J. McMichael, Alistair Woodward, Cameron Muir, Climate Change and the Health of Nations, →ISBN, page 67:
quote.text: Experience in Australia indicates that after a devastating weather event, up to one-fifth of people suffer the debilitating effects of extreme stress, emotional injury, and despair.

definitions.definition: One of several contests that combine to make up a competition.
An end result; an outcome (now chiefly in phrases).

quote.citation: 1624, Democritus Junior [pseudonym; Robert Burton], The Anatomy of Melancholy: […], 2nd edition, Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  John Lichfield and James Short, for Henry Cripps, →OCLC, partition 2, section 3, member 3:
quote.text: hard beginnings have many times prosperous events […].

quote.citation: 1707, Semele, by Eccles and Congrieve; scene 8
quote.text: Of my ill boding Dream / Behold the dire Event.

quote.citation: 1743, [Edward Young], “Night the Fourth. The Christian Triumph.”, in The Complaint: Or, Night-Thoughts on Life, Death, and Immortality, London:  […]  R[obert] Dodsley, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: dark doubts between the promise and event

quote.citation: 1985, Miss Marple: The Moving Finger, spoken by Mr. Pye (Richard Pearson):
quote.text: Miss Burton, you are an event! Sleepy, old Lymston's going to love you! Bye-bye. Bye.

definitions.definition: (physics) A point in spacetime having three spatial coordinates and one temporal coordinate.

(computing) A possible action that the user can perform that is monitored by an application or the operating system (event listener). When an event occurs an event handler is called which performs a specific task.
(probability theory) A set of some of the possible outcomes; a subset of the sample space.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) An affair in hand; business; enterprise.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Measure for Measure”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: Leave we him to his events.

definitions.definition: (medicine) An episode of severe health conditions.

quote.citation: 1590, Robert Greene, Greene’s Never Too Late, in The Life and Complete Works in Prose and Verse of Robert Greene, Volume 8, Huff Library, 1881, p. 33,[1]
quote.text: […]  I will first rehearse you an English Historie acted and evented in my Countrey of England  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete, intransitive) To be emitted or breathed out; to evaporate.

quote.citation: c. 1597, Ben Jonson, The Case is Altered, Act V, Scene 8, in C. H. Herford and Percy Simpson (editors), Ben Jonson, Volume 3, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1927, p. 178,[2]
quote.text:
ô that thou sawst my heart, or didst behold
The place from whence that scalding sigh evented.

quote.citation: 1615, William Barclay, Callirhoe; commonly called The Well of Spa or The Nymph of Aberdene‎[3], Aberdeen, published 1799, page 12:
quote.text: This is the reason why this water hath no such force when it is carried, as it hath at the spring it self: because the vertue of it consisteth in a spiritual and occulte qualitie, which eventeth and vanisheth by the carriage.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To expose to the air, ventilate.

quote.citation: 1559, attributed to William Baldwin, “How the Lorde Clyfford for his straunge and abhominable cruelty came to as straunge and sodayne a death” in The Mirror for Magistrates, Part III, edited by Joseph Haslewood, London: Lackington, Allen & Co., 1815, Volume 2, p. 198,[4]
quote.text:
For as I would my gorget have undon
To event the heat that had mee nigh undone,
An headles arrow strake mee through the throte,
Where through my soule forsooke his fylthy cote.
